newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Paris Club members to cut Zambia debt 67 percent.
newsitem.headline: Paris Club members to cut Zambia debt 67 percent.

text.p: Paris Club members will reduce Zambia's debt by 67 percent following the country's successful implementation of the Economic Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF), Finance Minister Ronald Penza said on Wednesday.

Penza said Paris Club members would cut the country's debt following endorsement by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) of Zambia's economic performance under ESAF at a mid-term review meeting held last week.

"The successful outcome of last Friday's mid-term review will now pave the way for Zambia to formalise the agreement which was reached last year with the Paris Club for a 67 percent reduction in Zambia's external debt service obligations to Paris Club members," Penza said in a statement.
The Paris Club includes Austria, Brazil, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Penza said key achievements leading to the favourable outcome of the IMF meeting included the reduction of inflation to the lowest annual level in eight years at 35 percent, and a 6.5 percent economic growth in 1996.
Other achievements included an increase in social sector spending at 34.5 percent, and progress in the privatisation of state-run enterprises.

"External financial stability was maintained with the value of non-traditional exports having continued their growth of over 15 percent so as to reach an impressive $230 million in 1996. The latter contributed to Zambia remaining current on its external debt payments," Penza said.
He added there was need for Zambia to reduce its external debt, to which vast resoruces were still being channelled, further during the course of the ESAF programme.
"On a per capita basis, Zambia is currently still spending four times as much on external debt service than it does on improving the health of its citizens," he said.
Zambia's total external debt stands at $6.38 billion.
Government aimed to access further debt relief from the recently apporved debt initiative for heavily-indebted poor countries for which Zambia had become eligible.

"Zambia's debt service-to-exports ratio could decline from 20 percent in 1996 to some 12 percent in the year 2000, thus significantly reducing the burden of external debt service on our economy and taking Zambia out of the external debt trap and firmly on the road towards higher export-led growth and greater poverty reduction," he said.
